title: Beginning Development
summary: Moving across the country to try to start game development
content: A little bit of over a year ago, I moved to Los Angeles and I had to restart my career from the ground up. When I first got here, I wasn't sure if I wanted to continue in the industry I had been in for five years or if I should take the time to explore my passions. My fiancee INSISTED on my passions, and it started with this one small project. The project that rekindled everything.I hadn't written a line of game code in a while when I started CyberCity Runner. Long enough that I'd forgotten the basics. I spent the first week reading documentation, Unity forums, and old projects just to remember how to flip a sprite based on input direction. What came out of it was an infinite scroller where you fight off an alien invasion while dodging spikes through the streets of a future city. Nothing revolutionary. But it ran at a consistent 60 FPS, the enemy AI spawned correctly, and I shipped it. The real win wasn't the game. It was proving to myself I could still do it. Key systems I built: adaptive enemy spawn logic, 2D sprite animation state machine, object pooling for shots and enemies, collision detection between projectiles and NPCs.

title: Order Up!
summary: Reverse engineering a classic - a bartending frog, very thirsty weirdos, and my first real deep dive into 2D
content: To continue on a semi-linear story, my next project was Tapped Out, and its inspiration came when I found Tapper at an arcade bar on a date night. I stood there for twenty minutes watching the game loop, sinking quarter after quarter into the machine to study the iterations. Until it hit — I can see exactly how this was built. I needed to build it myself. Tapped Out is my reverse-engineered reimagining of the classic. You play as a bartending frog managing five bars full of increasingly impatient customers. The design challenge was making customers feel alive — not just moving sprites but entities with needs that affected the whole environment. The solution was a behavior state system: thirsty, waiting, drinking, drunk. Each state didn't just change what the NPC did — it changed what every other NPC could do. A drunk customer hogging a seat blocked a new thirsty customer from entering. A chair that moved with its customer left a gap that changed the whole bar's rhythm. The insight that made it work: when a customer enters the drunk state, their chair resets to its origin after deletion. One rotating pool of chairs, one rotating cycle of customers. The same principle — recycling references instead of creating new ones — showed up later in my object pooling work on CyberCity Runner. Good solutions travel. This was also my first real dive into 2D tilemapping. It clicked when I started thinking about sorting layers the way I'd think about depth in 3D. Which object is closest to the camera. Which is farthest. Out of sight, out of my CPU.

title: Mystery is afoot!
summary: Project Dunwell begins development, the first thing on the list is level design.
content: "The message came in at 2:47 a.m. I read it at 6:12. Three hours and twenty-five minutes. In this city, that's not a window. That's a eulogy." That's the opening of Project Dunwell — a neo-noir sci-fi murder mystery I've been building in Unity with Ink handling all the branching dialogue. You play Marcus Dunwell. Not a detective. Not a cop. A former infrastructure engineer who helped design a civic surveillance network, got laid off when droids took his contracts, and kept a backdoor into the city's systems before he left. For safety reasons. He gets a message from someone who says he found something in the walls. Marcus reads it three hours too late. The apartment is locked from the inside. No windows. No balcony. One exit. A man tied to a wooden chair with a bag over his head and blood pooling on the floor. And a wall screen still glowing even though the power was cut. The villain never appears on screen. The player assembles him from his own mistakes — a login timestamp, a network signature, a corporate letterhead on a neighbor's door. Three endings. Nine clues. One question underneath all of it: what do you do when you helped build something that became a weapon? Six weeks ago this was a prose draft and a design document. Monday I'll show you what it looks like now.

title: Get a clue
summary: From GDD to working prototype, Project Dunwell takes shape
content: Six weeks ago Project Dunwell was a prose draft and a Word document. This is what it looks like now. Marcus Dunwell is moving through The Studios apartment building in Sificity. He has a voice — world-weary, precise, dry. He notices everything and editorializes nothing. When he walks up to Dexter's door and hears that the room sounds hollow, he says so. When he finds the body, he doesn't panic. He observes. Here's what's working: Nine clues placed across three beats, each one triggering its own Ink knot and delivering Marcus's observation in real time. Discovery order doesn't matter — find the gun before the body, find the fine notice before you understand what it means. The scene holds up either way. A building manager with three distinct dialogue states depending on what Marcus knows. A bluff mechanic where the wrong answer doesn't just fail — it ends the investigation entirely. A dialogue system built on Ink's branching architecture, integrated with Unity so that what Marcus knows changes what every character will and won't say. A case board where clues become cards and connections become revelations. I've been building this as a portfolio centrepiece — a project that puts gameplay programming, tools development, and narrative design in one place. But more than that it's a story I actually wanted to tell. About surveillance. About what you build with good intent and what it becomes without you. If you found evidence that implicated you in something you didn't do — would you use it or bury it?

title: Play Project Dunwell
summary: Project Dunwell is now Playable on itch.io and local machines
content:
Nine weeks ago Project Dunwell was a prose draft in a Word document. Today, you can play it. Project Dunwell is a neo-noir sci-fi murder mystery I built in Unity with Ink handling all the branching dialogue. You play Marcus Dunwell, not a detective, but an engineer who will find himself as the prime suspect. Summoned by the victim for Dunwell's history in infrastructure, each piece of evidence has his name and fingerprints on it, all captured with a surveillance system he designed. I built this as the centrepiece of my portfolio - a project that puts gameplay programming, tools development and narrative design in one place: 
> A 3D clue inspection system where you examine evidence in your hands 
> A player-driven case board that unlocks dialogue as you connect clues 
>A reactive Ink dialogue system where what Marcus knows changes every conversation 
>Three endings, each a different answer to the same question But it's more than a portfolio piece. It's a story I wanted to tell — about surveillance, about complicity, about the distance between what you build with good intent and what it becomes without you. This is what I want to do. Build games where systems and story are inseparable. Where the code serves the narrative and the narrative justifies the code. If you play it, tell me which ending you found.

title: Avast ye Matey
summary: Hoist the sails and set to Starboard
content: I shipped my fifth game and here's what I learned building ship combat in 12 days. Toxic Piracy is my submission for the Made to Be Played jam. The theme was TOXIC, and I wanted nautical combat that felt weighty, not floaty. A 3D world through an orthographic lens, where turning the ship felt like turning a rudder, not sliding a sprite. The biggest technical challenge was enemy broadside combat. Pirates don't shoot from the bow — they fire from the side. So when an enemy enters firing range, it needs to rotate 90 degrees relative to the player, not face them directly. I used dot products to determine which side — port or starboard — was already closer to facing the player, then locked that rotation in so the enemy committed to its broadside rather than jittering between sides. The other challenge was ship feel. I built a ramp and decay system for both steering and thrust — acceleration builds while you hold input, then bleeds off when you release. The ship drifts to a stop instead of snapping. Combined with kinematic Rigidbody collision against islands and bounce-back off enemy ships using contact normals, the result feels like a ship on water rather than a box on a plane. Built solo in Unity/C# in 12 days.

title: Scrubbing through my HDD
summary: Rediscovering old work, sharing it in a new way
content:
Dusting off one of my earliest Unity projects: a VR art gallery I built in 2017 for the Oculus Rift. I knew I wanted to make games then, and VR was the way to challenge myself. One laptop and two PC overhauls later, I found the build cleaning up old drives. 
On Display is an interactive museum featuring 25 works from a collaborating mixed-media artist. Paintings, sculptures, skateboards, video installations, and handbuilt physical objects, all translated from real-world art into a walkable VR space. Players can grab certain objects off the walls and display cases to inspect them up close using Oculus Touch controllers. 
This was my first time working with VR locomotion, Blender-to-Unity model pipelines, and shader/material work to make different surfaces: canvas, ceramic, iron, wood, video screens read correctly under VR lighting. 
It's rough by my current standards, but it shipped and it works. Adding it to the portfolio alongside my recent projects.

title: CyberCity Goes Mobile
summary: Making browser games playable on mobile
content:
I recently took CyberCity Runner, a game I shipped last year as a desktop infinite runner, and rebuilt it for mobile and WebGL. 
The interesting part wasn't porting it. It was rethinking how the controls communicate on a touchscreen. Desktop had keyboard input: instant, binary, no ambiguity. Mobile needed hold-to-run buttons that feel responsive without being twitchy, which meant implementing IPointerDownHandler and IPointerUpHandler on custom UI components instead of mapping touch to keyboard emulation. The player should never feel like they're fighting a touchscreen adaptation of a keyboard game. 
The other half was performance. Object pooling was already in place, but WebGL and mobile targets exposed optimization gaps that desktop hardware was hiding. Rebuilt the spawn pipeline, tightened the pool sizing, and got it holding at around 30 FPS on mobile hardware through browser gameplay. 
Same game, completely different engineering under the hood. Playable now on mobile and in-browser.

title: Hunting for Jobs
summary: Taking the CTRL + F out of life's challenges
content:
Six weeks into my job search, my tracking system was a single markdown file. It worked until it didn't. I could see the structure I'd built, but I'd lost the ability to actually trust it. Which applications needed a follow-up? Which ones had gone quiet? I was Ctrl-F searching my own life. 
So I built a REST API to fix it. Java, Spring Boot, JPA, PostgreSQL; deployed and live, and it's what actually runs my job search now instead of describing it. A few things I didn't expect going in: 
→ JpaRepository.save() will silently insert a new row instead of failing when an update target doesn't exist — unless you check findById() first. Found that one the hard way. 
→ Railway hands you a Postgres connection string in a format Spring's datasource doesn't accept out of the box. Building the JDBC URL from individual env vars instead of the combined one was the fix. 
→ Migrating data between local and deployed environments is its own small problem — I ended up writing a short script just to move records between the two without ID collisions. 
Six years in Unity and C# taught me one language deeply. This was my first backend-only project outside a game engine — no MonoBehaviours, no game loop, just a request lifecycle and a schema I actually cared about getting right.

title: Retrying learning Unreal
summary: Taking one engines practices and ideas, and implementing them in another
content:
Between job applications I've been exploring and building a hide-and-seek gameplay prototype in Unreal Engine using C++; my second Unreal project, translating six years of Unity/C# experience into a new engine. 
This iteration of ZoneClear is a spy-themed crowd search prototype. The player hunts for a target hidden among decoys, first in a casino, then in a nightclub. Each zone ramps up the difficulty, decoys blend closer to the target as camouflage tightness increases, and the crowd gets denser. 
What's under the hood: 
> Four custom C++ gameplay classes where population spawning is driven by UDataAssets, weighted decoy selection, and line trace interaction with component-based routing. The gap remains the biggest learning curve. 
> Dynamic material instances tinting each decoy at spawn time, lerping between a base color and the target's color based on a per-zone difficulty float. This was something I had planned in the Unity version, but material instancing felt better in Unreal. 
> A delegate-driven UI pipeline. C++ broadcasts an FText payload through a dynamic multicast delegate, Blueprint receives it and displays the narrative fragment on screen. Bare bones for now but something to polish and study with further iteration 
> Zone gating, which means finding the target hides the door, populates the next zone, and delivers the story beat in one event chain. Something I nailed down in Unity felt unfamiliar again in Unreal. Not anymore. 
The biggest lesson from this build: gameplay architecture transfers across engines. Not easily, but with practice. Data-driven spawning, component interaction routing, event-driven UI; these are the same design problems in different syntax. The Unreal-specific learning was in the details: forward declarations vs full includes, BeginPlay timing on spawned actors, CDO crashes from stale binaries, and when to use Live Coding vs a full rebuild. 
This is a portfolio prototype, not a shipped game, but every system here was built from scratch in C++, not visual scripting, and the patterns are production-ready.
